text: Every ServiceNow instance running Incident, Service Mapping, and Portfolio Management at the same time needs those modules to agree on what a service actually is. In this lesson we cover why ServiceNow had to publish a standard model — the Common Service Data Model, or CSDM — instead of leaving that up to each implementation.

Before CSDM existed as a published standard, ServiceNow didn't enforce one way to represent a service, an application, or the infrastructure under it. ITSM, ITOM, and Service Portfolio Management each grew their own expectations for that data, and every implementation team made its own judgment calls about table usage and relationships. Chapters 1 and 2 built CIs and relationships in a clean, self-contained example — a real instance has to make that same data work across all three of those modules at once.

That inconsistency carried a real cost. Inside one instance, data shaped for ITSM's expectations didn't always match what Service Portfolio Management needed a service record to look like, so dashboards built for one module would misread or miss records meant for another. Across customers, every implementation partner re-derived its own structure from scratch, so lessons learned on one engagement rarely transferred to the next, and admins relearned a bespoke model every time they changed employers.

CSDM is ServiceNow's real, published, vendor-maintained answer: a documented reference framework for how CIs, applications, and services relate to each other, meant to be followed consistently rather than invented independently each time. It gives ITSM, ITOM, and Service Portfolio Management a shared vocabulary to read and write against, and gives implementers a well-tested starting structure instead of a blank page. You don't have to guess what correct looks like — CSDM documents it.

From here forward in this course, the structures you build will follow CSDM's vocabulary instead of the ad hoc shapes used in Chapters 1 and 2. That's not complexity added for its own sake. It's the difference between CMDB data only one person understands, and CMDB data that ITSM, ITOM, and Service Portfolio Management can all actually use without a custom translation layer in between.
Next, we'll look at how CSDM actually organizes that data — the layered domains that separate what's still being planned from what's already live in production, and why that separation matters.
